name: Dusty Plum
lede: Dusty Plum is a dusty shade of [[plum|plum]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body: Dusty Plum joins the modifier *dusty* to the base color [[plum]], the fruit-named purple-red [1][4]. It appears in our core color set and in Ridgway and ISCC-NBS, but not in the separate commercial-and-design library we draw from for paint and print brands[1][2]. The ISCC-NBS system calls the matching block 'grayish reddish purple,' a Delta-E of 7.6 from this article's value [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[dark-hyssop-violet]], [[dusky-auricula-purple]] and [[slate-purple]], at 4.7, 5 and 5.1 ΔE [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 0.26% of 23,781 paintings, 62 paintings; within a single canvas it reads as a distinct area in 30 of them[3]. That makes it rarer than 57% of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, found in 0.6% of that century's 1,674 paintings, 3.2 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, by lightness rank, in 53% of its 30 appearances [3]. No painter in our archive stands out against the museum baseline for it [3]. The earliest dated appearance is a 1375 painting by Agnolo Gaddi, 537 years before the name's first documented record in 1912; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [3]. In printed English the word peaks in the 2010s and rose fastest in the 1980s, counting every sense of the word [3].
